div.p: Welcome to the methodology section of the PLO. In this section you will learn the theory about our Odoo Implementation Methodology, but mostly you will practice yourself with a ficticious project and your onboarder.
A standard implementation for an SME is divided into 3 main phases: Presales phase, Kick-off phase, implementation phase.

It is very important to choose the right projects from the beginning. Not all projects are good for you. Decide what kind of project you want to do (full standard or not, any type of a​ctivity or a specific industry, a short or long project, etc.).

p.span: From this point on you can organise a qualification meeting to prepare a demo for your potential future customer. Explore Odoo's industry-specific solutions; they could be helpful ( example).

div.p: The goal of this phase is to understand the client’s needs by asking “why” and actively listening. Take the necessary time and avoid rushing.

li.span: Internal Kick-off (sales): The team first meets with the salesperson to understand the sales process, client stakeholders, business workflows, and potential risks. This ensures better preparation before the external kick-off. The salesperson also helps the client prepare, for example, by creating flowcharts.
External Kick-off (customer): This meeting with the client is divided into three key parts:
Alignment / methodology: Define the way of working, identify the SPoC (Single Point of Contact), validate the methodology, and focus on priorities for a faster go-live.
Business Analysis: Analyze current workflows ("AS IS") instead of replicating existing systems. Guide the client strategically to gather key information and identify opportunities early.
Roadmap: Establish a phased implementation plan, prioritizing essential features first (MVP principle) to ensure a quick go-live and reduce failure risks.

div.p: This phase ensures users are onboarded efficiently, on time, and within budget by implementing in phases, staying close to standard configurations, and focusing on essentials (MVP).

p.strong: The sooner the system is used, the higher the success rate.

li.span: Import Data: Only import essential data (master and ongoing data); avoid historical data to save time and cost.
Implement in Phases: Prioritize must-haves and quick wins, regularly test configurations, and avoid unnecessary customizations to reduce costs and ease future upgrades.
Onboard Users: Ensure users are trained, ideally by the SPoC, and monitor their adaptation to the system.
Go Live: Plan a specific date, test all workflows beforehand, and conduct a progress review post-launch to assess adoption, improve collaboration, and explore next steps.
Push to Support: After completion, clients contact Odoo support. Proper documentation ensures smooth transitions for future improvements or reassignments.

div.p: A phasing is your road map to implement your project. It gives the order in which you will integrate the flows/applications.
But, why do we phase a project?

ul.li: We don’t start a trip without a map!

If you implement without a phasing, it emphasizes the risk of failure: We phase the project and focus on phases one by one to boost efficiency by avoiding that the project moves in plenty of directions and becomes out of control.
This phasing is your guideline in order to keep a macro view of your project
We bring phases to production one by one to validate the steps of the project sequentially and avoid discovering major issues at the end of the project.

div.p: In this section, you will discover how to phase your project.
Here is the link to the presentation to be discussed with your onboarder: How to phase, budget and plan a project?

The phasing aims to be able to go-live with a part of the system after the implementation and if possible in a limited amount of time and budget. You define the phasing and the SPoC has to validate it.

strong.em: ​ ​ ​ Your objective is to: "Onboard the USERS on TIME & on BUDGET"

div.p: In order to reach this goal, each phase will be defined by Minimum Viable Product (MVP) and/or 2nd Deployment.
You have to define which Minimum Viable Product flow you will have to implement first, in order for the customer to benefit as quickly as possible from the added value of using Odoo.
Here are some examples of phasing:

td.p: MVP : Sales, invoicing, purchase, inventory, manufacturing, website & E-commerce

div.p: What you must keep in mind is that you need to prove, during the early stage of the project, the added value of Odoo and the quality of the implementation service received. So you should focus on the scope that will make the biggest impact in the way the company operates. However, keep in mind that there is no magic phasing, and your best ally is your common sense. You can have 2 projects with the same scope but with different MVP phasing.

The phasing will be decided based on the information we gather during the kick-off phase. Here are some information you may collect during the Kick-Off that should help you on the way to design the phasing

ul.li: Which flow is related to the company's core business
Which departments will be involved in the change
License of the current system will expire
One of the employee will leave soon and s.he was the only one to know the workflow
The client urgencies. This point needs to be challenged. This is the BA's responsibility to assess if this is an urgency/need or not. Eg: accounting closing, website for a roadshow, etc.
The customer is losing efficiency or risks receiving fines because of an existing software, …

div.p: The phasing is different from the implementation steps. It gives vision to the customer about the way the project will evolve whereas the implementation is part of a phase. Implementing aims to put in place the needs of the client for him to be at the end of the phase ready to use Odoo in production.

div.h4: Switch from One Phase MVP/2nd Deployment to another one
div.p: You need to be sure that the previous MVP/2nd Deployment is completed before starting the next one. A phase is completed only once the go-live has happened and you and your customer agreed that they don't need further support and can focus on the work for the next phase.

If you start a new phase without having closed the previous one, clients might not want to take the jump to go-live and might try to postpone the go-live (eg: as all flows are not yet ready) or won’t let you start the next phase (eg: because there is still a lot to Improve).

Pay attention to the go-live and Post-Production parts of a MVP/2nd Deployment. The users will have feedback that you might have to work on to make sure that they will improve their way of working with Odoo. Plan some time right after the launch into production to be able to collect the feedback, decide if it needs to be implemented directly or if you need to plan that in a next phase. Keep challenging your customer to only work on blocking points that prevent them from using the system, and not on points that are working but could be improved. With the time & usage, those requests might be removed as they are no longer needed.

Once you start working on the next phase, you might still receive some requests for improvement. Make sure that the impact of managing them instead of working on the next phase is clear in the customer's mind (delay for the implementation, increase of the budget...) and make some decisions accordingly.
As you create the phasing, it is essential to estimate a budget for each of the MVP/ 2nd Deployment.

The budget is a tool which will help the consultant to define what he will be able to deliver in the context of the project. The budget is always an estimation, no matter the level of analysis that was done, it is never a fixed price. Furthermore, you don’t have to implement everything the client wants inside the budget. In a lot of cases, the amount of hours taken by the client is not sufficient to implement a full scope. Prioritizing is thus very important!

div.class: o_editor_banner o_not_editable lh-1 d-flex align-items-center alert alert-info pb-0 pt-3

div.p: The aims of budgeting are the followings :

ul.li: Monitor the project evolution and to take decisions / challenge the customer
Align Budget, Business Analysis & Customer expectations ; rather than sticking to the initial plan. Reassess the plan if needed !

div.p: Do not forget:

ul.li: The budget and the planning should be reassess if needed ;

div.p: There are 2 main approaches to budget a project.
The goal is to anticipate the different tasks you'll have to do, compute how many hours you will need and fit this into your budget.
Here is a tool to help you.

The point here is to take the number of hours of the pack and to split it among the different phases. You then compute how many meetings per phase you would have, the time to prepare those meetings and the post meeting time (project management but also functional investigations). Finally, you see if the number of meetings is enough to cover the MVP you agreed on with the client. If it's not enough then it means that the number of hours is too low to implement the full scope of the project. You'll then have to set priorities!

div.class: o_editor_banner o_not_editable lh-1 d-flex align-items-center alert alert-warning pb-0 pt-3

div.p: You don't need to allocate all the hours of the pack to the different phases. Keep some buffer time. It can be used later for a Q&A on other apps or if you need some additional time for a phase.
The opposite is true as well : It's not because the client bought a 25 hour a pack that you will be able to implement everything within that time.
Once your phasing is ready, you can plan it! How much time will each phase take ? It is important to estimate some dates in order to frame the project and set some time measures.

Note that adding some buffers and post go-live time is also important. Keep in mind that the planning will evolve throughout the project. You should stick to it, but sometimes we all know that some unexpected events will change your dates. Don’t be stressed about it! Just be transparent with your client if this changes!

div.class: o_editor_banner o_not_editable lh-1 d-flex align-items-center alert alert-info pb-0 pt-3

div.p: Don't forget to anticipate holidays. Add some buffer and post-go live time!
Communicating a timeline for a phasing is really important as it allows your customer to have the same vision as yours about his project and so having him more committed.
You will share the phasing, budget and planning of the project with your client in the second phase of the Kick off meeting. You will find more information regarding this in the next course.

div.class: o_editor_banner o_not_editable lh-1 d-flex align-items-center alert alert-info pb-0 pt-3

div.p: The phasing is a discussion between you and your customer. You keep the lead on it but it’s important that the client agrees on it and that (s)he understands the consequences of it.

div.h4: How to deal with scope creep?

div.class: o_editor_banner o_not_editable lh-1 d-flex align-items-center alert alert-info pb-0 pt-3

div.p: Scope creep definition : when your client adds more and more features as meetings progress.

You'll notice it with some clients : as the meetings progress they add will more and more features for you to implement. This will enlarge the scope of the implementation, and eventually, you'll notice that you're not on on time and on budget anymore. First of all, the "ABC rule" (Always be Challenging) always applies! It's important for you to always challenge the request of the client.

Second point, if challenging the client is not working, just have a conversation with him/her about it. Tell them that if we keep going like this, we will not respect the budget and that it will have to be increased. Other option: we drop a few features.

div.p: From the business needs identified, you need to determine the ones that will have the biggest positive impact on the company and, thus, will be implemented first.

ul.li: The added value for the company: represents the ability for your employee to do more in less time
The ease of transformation: how fast or easy it is to digitize the process to get potential impact

div.p: We can identify 4 types of impact:

ul.li: Game changer: the implementation of this flow will be more complex and/or take a lot of time. But it will have a high positive impact on the company. You need to consider to implement this flow while planning enough time for it.
Quick Win: Implementing this flow is quite easy and has an high added value for the company. You should definitely start by implementing these flows.

Fine tuning: These are flows easy to implement but with a low impact on the company. These should be kept of the end of the implementation if the client is willing to go further in the functionalities.
To avoid: The impact of these flows is low for the company and they are difficult to put in place. As the name indicates, you should avoid implementing it.

div.p: Now that the first phase of your project is defined, it’s time to present the process flows of this phase to your customer. Keep these tips in mind:

ul.li: Tell a user story: Use real customer data and refer to actual users by name. Put yourself in the shoes of one user at a time to make the flow relatable and concrete.
Start with the result: Show the final outcome first. Dive into the configurations only after the customer has validated the flow—this might not happen in the same session.
Be prepared: Expect some resistance from the customer, both to change in general and to the specific solution you’re proposing.
